title: Distributed locking
problem: Two workers on different machines both believe they hold the lock for the same job, and the one whose lease silently expired writes last.
summary: A distributed lock grants one holder at a time across machines, usually a TTL key in Redis or a consensus store. The TTL can expire under a slow holder, so a correct lock needs a fencing token the resource checks, or no lock at all.
catTip: I sit on the warm server and declare it mine, then nap for forty seconds. When I wake, another cat is sitting there too: my claim expired while I slept. A lock with a TTL is a lease, and a lease needs a fencing token.

recall.q: A worker holding a Redis lock with a 30-second TTL pauses for 40 seconds and then writes. What goes wrong, and what prevents it?
recall.a: The key expired during the pause, another worker acquired the lock, and both write. The TTL makes the lock a lease whose expiry the holder cannot see; a fencing token checked by the storage rejects the late write, and a compare-and-delete release stops the first worker deleting the second worker's lock.

guide.breaks: A lock key with a TTL expires while its holder is paused or slow, a second worker takes the lock and both write to the same resource; a plain DEL on release can also remove a lock that now belongs to someone else.
guide.tradeoffs: Every distributed lock is a lease, so you pay either for a consensus round trip plus a fencing check on the resource, or you accept that under pauses and clock shifts two holders can briefly overlap.
guide.explainSimply: A distributed lock is a hotel key card that expires at check-out, so a room is never stuck forever if a guest disappears. The catch is that an oversleeping guest does not notice the card has expired, and the next guest is let in while they are still inside. A safe system has the room itself check whose turn it is.
guide.hint: Think about what the holder knows at the moment its lease expires, and who else could do the checking.

meow: Meow-tual exclusion: my spot on the server expires while I nap. Fence it, or purr-haps two cats write at once.

quiz.prompt: A worker acquires a Redis lock with SET NX PX 30000, then stalls for 45 seconds in a garbage-collection pause before writing. Which statement is correct?
options: Redis notices the worker is paused and extends the lock until it finishes
The lock expired during the pause, another worker may hold it, and only a check on the storage side such as a fencing token can reject the late write
The compare-and-delete release script prevents the double write because the token no longer matches
Redlock would prevent this because a majority of five nodes must agree before the key expires
quiz.explanation: Expiry is time-based and invisible to the holder, so only the resource can refuse the stale write. The compare-and-delete script protects the release step, stopping the late worker from deleting someone else's lock, not the write.

quiz.prompt: Which alternative removes the need for a distributed lock when the goal is to run a nightly job exactly once?
options: Insert a row keyed by job and date under a unique constraint and let the loser's insert fail
Have every worker sleep a random time before starting so they rarely collide
Give the lock a longer TTL so the job always finishes before it expires
Replicate the Redis lock key to a replica so it survives a primary failure
quiz.explanation: A unique constraint makes the database choose exactly one winner atomically. A longer TTL only moves the failure to a longer pause, and random delays merely make collisions less likely.

cards.q: Why must a Redis lock be released with a compare-and-delete script rather than a plain DEL?
cards.a: A client whose lock has already expired may run DEL and remove the lock another client now holds, letting a third client in. Comparing the stored random token first means a late release finds a different token and does nothing.

cards.q: Kleppmann and antirez disagreed about Redlock. Name one point of disagreement and one point of agreement.
cards.a: Disagreement: whether a majority of independent Redis nodes is a safe correctness lock given wall-clock expiry and pauses (Kleppmann: no; antirez: yes, given bounded clock drift). Agreement: a holder paused after acquiring cannot know its lease expired, so the resource must check a token, and Redis should expire keys on a monotonic clock.

sources.title: Redis documentation, "Distributed Locks with Redis" (single-instance recipe and the Redlock algorithm)
sources.supports: SET resource NX PX 30000 with a random value; the compare-and-delete Lua script and DELEX IFEQ in Redis 8.4; Redlock with N=5 masters, majority of three, validity minus elapsed time and drift, random retry delay; asynchronous replication failover race; the fsync-every-second default and delayed restarts; the disclaimer about fencing tokens and wall-clock expiry

sources.title: Redis documentation, SET command
sources.supports: NX sets only if the key does not exist and returns a null reply otherwise; PX sets a millisecond expiry

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann, "How to do distributed locking" (8 February 2016)
sources.supports: efficiency versus correctness locks; the GC-pause scenario; fencing tokens as monotonically increasing numbers rejected by the storage (tokens 33 and 34); the critique that Redlock issues no fencing tokens and depends on wall-clock timing; the recommendation of a single Redis node for efficiency and a consensus system with fencing for correctness

sources.title: Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez), "Is Redlock safe?" (2016)
sources.supports: the reply: pauses after acquisition affect every auto-releasing lock; Redlock assumes bounded clock drift rather than synchronised clocks; delays before acquisition are caught by the validity check; the random token can be checked by the resource; agreement that Redis should use a monotonic clock

sources.title: Apache ZooKeeper, "ZooKeeper Recipes and Solutions", Locks
sources.supports: the lock recipe: ephemeral sequential child nodes, lowest sequence number holds the lock, watch only the next-lower node to avoid the herd effect, delete to release

sources.title: etcd documentation, "etcd concurrency API reference" (Lock service)
sources.supports: a lock is tied to a lease and is held until Unlock or until the lease expires or is revoked

sources.title: etcd source, client/v3/concurrency/mutex.go
sources.supports: the mutex writes a key under the lock prefix in a transaction guarded by CreateRevision equal to zero, attached to the session lease; the key with the lowest creation revision owns the lock; waiters wait for lower-revision keys to be deleted
